slides.title: OS Evolution
slides.body: OS Evolution
slides.notes: First of all we will be learning about the OS Evolution

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
The OS Evolution Timeline
1940s–50s
1960s
1970s
1980s
Manual operation
no OS
Serial processing
Simple batch systems
Multiprogramming
Early Multi-tasking (UNIX)
Personal computing
Early GUIs (Mac OS, Windows)
slides.notes: Now, let’s look at how operating systems evolved over time.In the 1940s and 50s, there were no modern operating systems, and programs were run manually using low-level instructions.In the 1960s, batch systems were introduced to automate job execution.In the 1970s, operating systems evolved with multiprogramming and multitasking, and UNIX introduced strong multi-user and time-sharing capabilities.\In the 1980s, personal computers became popular, and graphical interfaces like Mac OS and Windows made computers easier to use.

slides.notes: Moving on, from the 1990s, operating systems became widely networked with strong internet support.In the 2000s, mobile operating systems, virtualization, and cloud computing emerged.In the 2010s, technologies like IoT, containerization, and early AI integration became important.Today, operating systems continue to evolve with AI, distributed cloud systems, and edge computing, powering modern applications

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Early Computing: The No OS Era
No operating system, one program runs at a time
Direct machine-level programming
Manual operation using switches, punch cards
Programmer had complete control over hardware
slides.notes: Next, let's go back to the early days of computing, when operating systems didn't exist. Computers could run only one program at a time, and programmers interacted directly with the hardware using switches and punch cards(Punch cards were thick paper cards with holes in specific positions, where each pattern of holes represented data or instructions for the computer to read). While this gave complete control over the machine, it made computing slow, complex, and error-prone.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Why Did OS Emerge?
Early Computing Problems (1940s-1950s):
Problem 1: Hardware was EXPENSIVE and idle most of the time
Computers cost millions of dollars
Most of the time, it was doing nothing while waiting for the next task
slides.notes: Now, let's understand why operating systems became necessary. Early computers were extremely expensive, but they remained idle for long periods while waiting for the next task. This poor utilization of costly hardware highlighted the need for a system that could manage and keep the computer busy more efficiently.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Why Did OS Emerge?
Early Computing Problems (1940s-1950s):
Operators had to set up each job manually
Switching between programs took lots of time
The CPU stayed idle (not working) during this time
Problem 2: Humans were too slow to operate them
slides.notes: Next, another major challenge was the slow manual operation. Before every program, operators had to set up the system manually, and switching between jobs took a lot of time. During this entire process, the CPU remained idle, leading to inefficient use of the computer.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Why Did OS Emerge?
Early Computing Problems (1940s-1950s):
Problem 3: Programs were loaded by hand
Programs were loaded using switches, plugboards, or punch cards
Took a lot of time and caused many errors
slides.notes: Moving on, programs also had to be loaded manually using switches, plugboards, or punch cards. This process was time-consuming and prone to human errors, making program execution inefficient and unreliable.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Types of Operating Systems
Batch OS 
Multiprogramming OS
Multi-tasking OS
Multi-Processing OS 
Operating systems evolved step by step to solve growing challenges
Here are the main types of OS developed over time
Multi-User OS
Distributed OS
Real-Time OS
Network OS
Embedded OS
slides.notes: Now, let's explore the different types of operating systems. As computing needs evolved, operating systems also evolved to solve new challenges. We'll look at each type one by one, understand why it was introduced, and see where it is commonly used.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Batch Operating System (1960s)
A Batch Operating System groups similar jobs together and executes them sequentially without user interaction during the execution process
Batch Operating System
Use Cases
Payroll processing
Bank transaction processing
Large-scale scientific computation
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Batch Operating System, one of the earliest operating systems. It groups similar jobs into batches and executes them one after another without requiring user interaction during execution. This approach was widely used for repetitive tasks such as payroll processing, bank transactions, and large-scale scientific computations.

slides.title: Batch Operating System (1960s)
slides.body:
How Batch Operating System Works?

Batch

Batch

slides.notes: Moving on, let's see how a Batch Operating System works. Individual jobs are first collected and grouped into batches by the operating system.These batches are then sent to the CPU one after another for execution, without requiring any user intervention during the process.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Multiprogramming OS (1970s)
A Multiprogramming Operating System loads multiple programs into memory and runs them on a single processor by switching when one program waits for I/O, improving CPU usage by keeping it busy
Multiprogramming Operating System
Use Cases
Airline reservation systems
Government and corporate data centers
slides.notes: in memory at the same time. Whenever one program waits for an I/O operation, the CPU switches to another program, improving CPU utilization. This approach was widely used in airline reservation systems and large data centers.

slides.title: Multiprogramming Operating System (1970s)
slides.body:
How it Works
CPU

Main Memory
JOB A is doing I/O Operation
JOB B is IN Execution
JOB C, D, E, F  are Waiting for CPU
slides.notes: Now, let's see how multiprogramming works. Multiple jobs are loaded into the main memory together. If one job is waiting for an I/O operation, the CPU immediately switches to another ready job instead of staying idle. This keeps the CPU busy and improves overall system efficiency.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Multi-tasking Operating System
A Multi-tasking operating system allows a user to run multiple programs or tasks at the same time by rapidly switching the CPU between them
Multi-tasking Operating System
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Multi-tasking Operating System. It allows a single user to run multiple applications at the same time by rapidly switching the CPU between them. This creates the impression that all the programs are running simultaneously, making the system more responsive.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Multi-tasking Operating System
Unlike Multiprogramming, Multitasking uses time-based context switching allowing the CPU to switch between tasks at regular intervals, even if no task is waiting for I/O
Use Cases
Desktop OS (Windows, macOS, Linux)
Mobile devices
Multi-tasking Operating System
slides.notes: Moving on, unlike multiprogramming, multitasking switches the CPU between tasks at regular time intervals, even if no task is waiting for I/O. This provides a smooth user experience by allowing multiple applications to appear as if they're running simultaneously. It's commonly used in desktop and mobile operating systems.

slides.title: Multi-tasking Operating System
slides.body:
Time-Sharing OS
It is a multi-user extension of multitasking where CPU time is divided into fixed intervals called time slices (quantum). 
While multitasking focuses on a single user running multiple programs, time-sharing enables multiple users to interact with the system simultaneously, each receiving a fair share of CPU time
Time-sharing OS is a multi-user extension of multitasking where CPU time is divided into fixed time slices (quantum), allowing multiple users to interact with the system simultaneously, each receiving a fair share of CPU time
Use Cases
University labs (multiple students)
Cloud multi-user systems
Time-Sharing Operating System
slides.notes: Next, let's understand Time-Sharing Operating Systems. It extends the idea of multitasking to support multiple users. The CPU divides its time into small time slices and allocates them fairly among users, allowing everyone to interact with the system as if they have dedicated access.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Multi-user Operating System
A Multi-user Operating System enables multiple users to access and use a computer system concurrently, either remotely or locally
Multi-user
Operating System
Use Cases
Education and Universities
Banking and Financial Systems
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the Multi-user Operating System. It allows multiple users to access the same computer system simultaneously, either locally or over a network. Each user gets an independent working environment, making it ideal for universities, banks, and other organizations with many users.

slides.title: Multi-user Operating System
slides.body:
Multi-user Operating System
Central Computer OS
slides.notes: Now, let's see how a Multi-user Operating System works. A central computer running the operating system serves multiple client systems at the same time. It manages resources efficiently and ensures that each user can work independently without affecting others.

slides.title: Learning How OS Evolved
slides.body:
Multi-Processing Operating System
A Multi-Processing Operating System uses two or more CPUs (or CPU cores) within a single computer system to execute multiple processes truly simultaneously
Multi-Processing
Operating System
Use Cases
Scientific Computing & Simulations
Video and Graphics Rendering
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Multi-Processing Operating System. Unlike previous operating systems, it uses two or more CPUs or CPU cores to execute multiple processes simultaneously. This improves performance and is commonly used in scientific computing, simulations, and video or graphics rendering.

slides.title: Multi-Processing Operating System
slides.body:
How it Works
Memory
slides.notes: Moving on, this diagram shows how a multiprocessing system works. Each CPU has its own registers and cache, but they all share the same main memory. This allows multiple processors to execute different tasks simultaneously while accessing common data efficiently.

slides.title: Exploring Specialized Operating Systems
slides.body:
Real-Time Operating System (RTOS)
 A Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) guarantees a response to inputs or events within a fixed, predictable time limit (often called a "deadline")
Real-Time
Operating System
Use Cases
Industrial robot control systems
Aerospace applications
slides.notes: Next, let's discuss the Real-Time Operating System, or RTOS. It is designed to respond to events within a guaranteed time limit, making timely execution its highest priority. This makes RTOS ideal for time-critical applications such as industrial robots and aerospace systems.

slides.title: Real-Time Operating System (RTOS)
slides.body: How it Works?
slides.notes: Moving on, let's see how an RTOS works. User requests are handled by the application, which passes them to the RTOS. The RTOS then communicates with the hardware and ensures every task is completed within its specified deadline, providing fast and predictable responses.

slides.title: Exploring Specialized Operating Systems
slides.body:
Network Operating System (NOS)
A Network Operating System (NOS) provides services and manages resources across a network, enabling multiple computers to share files, printers, and applications
Network
Operating System
Use Cases
Enterprise Resource Sharing
Client-Server Management
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Network Operating System, or NOS. It manages resources across a network, allowing multiple computers to share files, printers, and applications efficiently. It is commonly used in enterprise environments and client-server systems where centralized resource management is important.

slides.title: Exploring Specialized Operating Systems
slides.body:
Distributed Operating System (DOS)
A Distributed Operating System (DOS) manages a group of interconnected computers (nodes) that work together as a single, coordinated system, allowing them to function efficiently as one entity
Distributed
Operating System
Use Cases
Cloud computing platforms (Google, AWS)
Distributed databases
slides.notes: Moving on, let's look at the Distributed Operating System. It connects multiple computers and manages them as if they were a single system. This enables efficient resource sharing and coordinated processing, making it ideal for cloud computing platforms and distributed databases.

slides.title: Distributed Operating System (DOS)
slides.body: Architecture of Distributed OS(DOS)
slides.notes: Now, let's see the architecture of a Distributed Operating System. Here, multiple computers, each with their own CPU, memory, and storage, are connected through a communication network. The operating system coordinates these nodes so they work together and appear as a single unified system to the user.

slides.title: Exploring Specialized Operating Systems
slides.body:
Embedded Operating System (EOS)
An embedded operating system runs on dedicated hardware for specific tasks and is optimized for efficiency and reliability
Embedded
Operating System
slides.notes: Finally, let's look at the Embedded Operating System. It is designed for dedicated devices that perform specific tasks and is optimized for efficiency, reliability, and low resource usage. Examples include smart appliances, medical devices, and automotive systems.

slides.title: Embedded Operating System (EOS)
slides.body:
Examples
Embedded Systems
ATMs
Smart TVs
Washing machines
Automotive systems
Fitness trackers
slides.notes: To conclude, embedded operating systems are found in many everyday devices. Common examples include ATMs, Smart TVs, washing machines, automotive systems, and fitness trackers, where they ensure efficient and reliable operation for specific tasks.

slides.title: OS Structure
slides.body: OS Structure
slides.notes: Now we will understand the OS Structure

slides.title: OS Structure
slides.body:
OS Structure
What is an OS Structure ?
OS structure defines how components are organized and interact
Simplifying the structure makes customization easier
Breaking the OS into parts, like solving smaller tasks, helps manage complexity
Components are integrated within the kernel to form a cohesive system
Operating System Structure
slides.notes: Now, let's understand what an Operating System Structure is. It defines how different OS components are organized and work together. By dividing the operating system into smaller components, it becomes easier to design, customize, maintain, and manage, while all these components work together through the kernel as a single system.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure 
Types of Structures
Monolithic Structure
Layered Structure
Microkernel Structure
Hybrid Structure
ExoKernel Structure
Client-Server Structure
Modular Structure
Virtual Machines Structure

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Monolithic Structure
High performance due to direct communication between components
All OS services (process management, memory management, file systems, etc.) are bundled into a single, large block of code running in kernel mode
Advantages
Difficult to maintain and debug due to its large size
Disadvantages
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the Monolithic OS Structure. In this structure, all core operating system services run together inside a single kernel. This provides high performance because components communicate directly, but it also makes the system harder to maintain and debug due to its large and tightly coupled design.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:

slides.notes: Moving on, this diagram shows the Monolithic Structure. Applications run in unprivileged mode, while all core services like memory management, ……..and drivers run together inside a single kernel in privileged mode, which directly interacts with the hardware. This direct interaction improves performance but also makes the kernel more complex to maintain.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Layered Structure
Simplifies debugging and maintenance by isolating errors to specific layers
Advantages
Adds overhead as data has to be passed through multiple layers
Disadvantages
The OS is divided into layers, where each layer depends on the services provided by the layer below it. The bottom layer is the hardware, and the topmost layer is the user interface
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Layered Structure. In this approach, the operating system is divided into multiple layers, where each layer uses the services of the layer below it. This makes the OS easier to debug and maintain, but passing data through multiple layers can introduce some performance overhead.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Layered Structure
Layer 0 Hardware
Layer1
Layer NUser Interface
slides.notes: Moving on, this diagram shows the Layered Structure. The hardware forms the bottom layer, and each higher layer builds on the services of the layer below it. The topmost layer is the user interface, allowing users to interact with the system in an organized and modular way.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Microkernel Structure
More modular, secure, and easier to maintain
Advantages
Slower due to added communication overhead between user space and kernel
Disadvantages
The kernel provides only basic services like inter-process communication, scheduling, and hardware abstraction. Other services, such as file systems and device drivers, run in user space
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Microkernel Structure. Here, the kernel handles only essential services like process scheduling, inter-process communication, and hardware abstraction, while services like file systems and device drivers run in user space. This makes the system more modular and secure, but communication between user space and the kernel can reduce performance.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Microkernel Structure
Application
Basic IPC,Virtual Memory Scheduling
Hardware
File Server
Unix Server

Application IPC
Microkernel Operating System
slides.notes: Moving on, this diagram shows the Microkernel Structure. Only essential services like IPC, scheduling, and virtual memory remain inside the kernel, while components such as device drivers, file servers, and UNIX services run separately in user space. This modular design improves security and maintainability.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Hybrid Structure
Provides a balance between performance and modularity
Advantages
Complex design and implementation
Disadvantages
Combines aspects of both monolithic and microkernel architectures, Some OS services run in user space (like in a microkernel), but others are included in the kernel for performance (like in a monolithic kernel)
slides.notes: Next, let's look at the Hybrid Structure.As the name suggests, it combines features of both Monolithic and Microkernel architectures.Performance-critical services are kept inside the kernel for speed, while some other services run in user space for better modularity and maintainability.This provides a balance between performance and modularity, but it also makes the design more complex.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Hybrid Structure
FileSystems
NetworkSubSystems
MemoryManagement
ProcessManagement
Drivers
Hardware

slides.notes: Moving on, this diagram shows the Hybrid Structure. Applications and some services run in user mode and communicate with the hybrid kernel through system calls. The kernel handles performance-critical components like scheduling, memory, processes, file systems, I/O, and core drivers, while directly interacting with the hardware. This design combines the performance of a monolithic kernel with the modularity of a microkernel.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Exokernel Structure
High performance and flexibility for applications
Advantages
Requires applications to handle most tasks, which can be complex and error-prone
Disadvantages
A minimal kernel that provides only the most basic services, like hardware access and resource management, while allowing applications to manage resources directly
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Exokernel Structure. It provides only basic services like hardware access and resource management, allowing applications to manage resources directly. This offers high performance and flexibility but also makes application development more complex.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Exokernel Structure
APPLICATION
KERNEL
LIBRARY
LIBRARY
LIBRARY
slides.notes: Moving on, this diagram shows the Exokernel Structure. The kernel provides only basic hardware access, while libraries offer higher-level services to applications. This allows applications to interact with hardware more directly, giving better performance and flexibility.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Modular Structure
Flexibility to add or remove components as needed
Advantages
Complexity in managing the interaction between modules
Disadvantages
OS components are divided into modules that can be loaded or unloaded dynamically, Each module handles specific tasks like networking, device management, etc
(modular kernel)
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Modular Structure. In this approach, the operating system is divided into independent modules, each responsible for a specific task, such as networking or device management. These modules can be loaded or unloaded dynamically, making the system flexible, although managing the modules adds some complexity.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure

slides.notes: Moving on, this diagram shows the Modular Structure. At the center is the core kernel, while components like the file system, device drivers, scheduling classes, stream modules, and system calls are organized as separate modules around it. These modules can be loaded or removed as needed, making the operating system flexible and easier to extend.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Client-Server Structure
Easy to scale and distribute across multiple machines
Advantages
Requires network management and adds communication overhead
Disadvantages
OS is structured around a client-server model, where clients (user programs) communicate with servers (kernel services) over a network or within the system
(with network services)
slides.notes:
Next, let's understand the Client-Server Structure.
In this model, user programs are called clients, and they request services from servers.
These servers provide operating system functions like handling files, memory, or devices.
This structure is easy to scale across multiple machines, but communication between clients and servers can cause some delay or overhead.

slides.title: Types of OS Structure
slides.body:
Types of OS Structure
Virtual Machine Structure
Isolation between different environments, allowing for testing, security, and resource efficiency
Advantages
Overhead of managing multiple virtual machines
Disadvantages
The OS creates and manages virtual machines, each with its own set of resources and OS environment
slides.notes: Next, let's understand the Virtual Machine Structure. In this approach, the operating system creates and manages multiple virtual machines, each with its own operating system and resources. This provides strong isolation for security and testing, but managing multiple virtual machines introduces additional overhead.

slides.title: Case Studies
slides.body: Case Studies
slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the Case Studies

slides.title: Case Study
slides.body:
Windows OS
Developed by Microsoft
Closed-source, proprietary operating system
Uses Hybrid Kernel architecture
Strong support for GUI, applications, and gaming
Widely used in personal computers and business environments
Offers strong backward compatibility
Includes built-in security tools like Windows Defender
slides.notes: Now, let's take Windows as a case study. Developed by Microsoft, it is a closed-source operating system that uses a hybrid kernel design. It is widely used in personal and business environments due to its strong GUI support, broad application compatibility, backward compatibility, and built-in security features like Windows Defender.

slides.title: Case Study
slides.body:
Key Features of Windows OS
User-friendly desktop interface
Extensive driver and hardware support
Supports multitasking and virtual memory
Frequent updates and patch management
Integration with Microsoft ecosystem (Office, OneDrive)
slides.notes: Next, let's look at some key features of Windows OS. It offers a user-friendly interface, supports a wide range of hardware and device drivers, enables multitasking with virtual memory, receives regular security updates, and integrates seamlessly with Microsoft services like Office and OneDrive.

slides.title: Case Study
slides.body:
Linux
Open-source and community-driven (various distributions)
Monolithic
Modular Kernel Architecture
Highly customizable and secure
Widely used in servers, cloud systems, networking, and development
Free to use and modify
Popular distros: Ubuntu, Fedora, Red Hat, Kali Linux
slides.notes: Moving on, let's take Linux as another case study. It is an open-source operating system that uses a monolithic modular kernel. Linux is highly customizable, secure, and widely used in servers, cloud computing, networking, and software development. Popular distributions include Ubuntu, Fedora, Red Hat, and Kali Linux.

slides.title: Case Study
slides.body:
Key Features of Linux
Strong command-line support
Flexible file system and permissions
Better performance & security for server environments
Supports multiple desktop environments
slides.notes: Next, let's explore some key features of Linux. It offers powerful command-line support, a flexible file system with strong permission management, excellent performance and security for server environments, and supports multiple desktop environments to suit different user preferences.

Hybrid Kernel
slides.notes: Now, let's look at macOS. Developed by Apple, it uses a hybrid kernel and is designed for Apple devices like MacBooks and iMacs. Based on Unix, macOS is known for its stability, security, smooth user experience, and high performance.

slides.title: Case Study
slides.body:
Key Features of MacOS
Good for video editing, music, and programming
Strong security and privacy protection
Works very well with other Apple devices (iPhone, iPad, Watch)
Comes with many useful apps already installed
Gets regular software updates
slides.notes: Finally, let's look at the key features of macOS. It integrates seamlessly with other Apple devices, offers strong security and privacy, is widely used for creative work and programming, comes with many built-in applications, and receives regular software updates.

slides.notes:
Next, let's look at operating systems used in handheld devices.
These operating systems are designed for smartphones and tablets.
They focus on providing a touch-friendly user interface, low power consumption, app-based functionality, and strong wireless connectivity like Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and 5G.
Common examples include Android OS, which is Linux-based, and iOS, which is Apple's proprietary operating system.

slides.title: Handheld Devices
slides.body:
Key Features
Uses less power to save battery
Supports many apps (App Store / Play Store)
Works with phone sensors like camera, GPS, motion sensor
Can update software through the internet
Secure login using fingerprint or face unlock
slides.notes: Finally, let's look at the key features of handheld operating systems. They are optimized for low power consumption, support a wide range of mobile apps,work seamlessly with built-in sensors like GPS and cameras, receive software updates over the internet, and provide secure authentication using fingerprint or face unlock.
